questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express

$$
f(x)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{4}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f={u}^{4},\,u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=4{u}^{3}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =4{u}^{3}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-4{u}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-4{cos}^{3}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-{csc}^{2}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-{csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x{csc}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Reciprocal Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Let $g(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x)$ and $h(x)=-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}.$ Then

$$
f(x)=g(x)+h(x).
$$

First, we differentiate $g(x).$ We express $g(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x)$ as the composite function

$$
g=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡u,\,u=2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u\cdot 2 \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate $h(x)=-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}.$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =-{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={g}^{′}(x)+{h}^{′}(x) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x)-{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=4\operatorname{sec}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=4\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =4\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$
